title: Tala Clapper
description: A circle of beat dots shows one cycle of a South Asian tala: Teentaal (16 beats), Rupak (7), Dadra (6) or the Carnatic Adi tala (8). Learners press Start to light each beat in turn, follow the clap, wave and finger-count gestures, adjust the tempo, and find sam, the first beat. Short synthesized WebAudio clicks, with a distinct low tone on sam, play only after the user presses Start.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: South Asian cultures
Music
Rhythm
Hindustani and Carnatic music
publisher: Roots & Rivers: An Interactive Guide to South Asian Cultures for High School Students
audience: Students, Educators, South Asian student club leaders
learningObjectives: Count through a full cycle of Teentaal, Rupak, Dadra and Adi tala.
Perform the clap, wave and finger-count gestures on the correct beats.
Identify sam, the first beat of the cycle, and khali, the wave, by sight and sound.
Compare how Hindustani and Carnatic musicians keep a tala with their hands.
prerequisites: Knowing that South Asia has northern (Hindustani) and southern (Carnatic) classical music traditions
keyQuestions: Where is sam in each tala, and how can you tell when it is coming?
Why does Rupak begin with a wave instead of a clap?
How does keeping Adi tala with finger counts differ from clapping Teentaal?
misconceptions: Indian classical music is improvised with no rules.
The first beat of a cycle is always the loudest.
Every tala has four beats per bar like most pop songs.
controls: Click or tap a beat dot
